extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century readers (gentlemen and ladies interested in manners, writing, gardening, and fashion)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of short instructive essays on conduct, style, and taste—covering method in writing and conversation, principles of garden design, and the social role of dress and fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the whole scheme of the discourse in your mind before you set pen to paper; range thoughts under proper heads so they grow out of one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: helps invention (new thoughts arise under each head), makes thoughts more intelligible, discovers the writer's drift, causes each thought to show in its greatest beauty, aids reader comprehension and long retention. Method is especially necessary for ordinary writers; irregularity is tolerable mainly for writers of great learning or genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular/essayistic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write without strict method when full of thought—throw down several thoughts together in the manner of Montaigne or Seneca.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces many noble objects rising among one another (a fruitful ramble) and can yield novel discoveries; anti-pattern: yields a confused, imperfect notion of the whole and is supportable only for men of great learning or genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method in conversation and debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage disputes with regularity: keep to the question, methodize thoughts, and avoid turning the argument into unrelated topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: running off the question, producing a 'barren superfluity of words' (Tom Puzzle). Recommended technique: cut tangents with a clarifying question (e.g., 'What then? We allow all this to be true, but what is it to our present purpose?'). A methodical, clear-headed speaker (Will Dry) gains advantage over verbose undisciplined disputants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and clarity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Use few words and a clear, methodical head to gain advantage in speech and debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Will Dry, whose concise questioning non-plusses verbose arguers; brevity helps concentrate on what is to be proved and exposes empty eloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garden composition: mixed, naturalistic design
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose gardens as an interwoven confusion of kitchen, parterre, orchard, and flower-garden to achieve a 'beautiful wildness' resembling nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overvalue rarity—include common field flowers transplanted into the garden; group the products of the same season together so they appear simultaneously and create a varied picture; irregular plantations can enhance variety and surprise the visitor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant species suited to soil and climate
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit into the garden only plants that naturally rejoice in the soil; avoid forcing tender foreign plants into unsuitable conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for hardy, naturally-suited species; kitchen-garden produce and native growths preferred over delicate exotics that require artificial heat (orangery) and are less fitting to the place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water-features should mimic natural courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Design fountains and streams to form a wandering rill that visits most plantations and runs as it would in an open field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the water flow through banks of violets, primroses, and other plants so the feature appears natural and contributes to the pleasure and plenty of the place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect birds and encourage wildlife
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not destroy birds' nests in spring or drive birds away in fruit-time; value a garden for its bird-life as much as for its fruit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing springs, shades, solitude, and shelter invites birds; the music of the season (blackbirds, thrushes, jays) is a central garden pleasure and justifies withholding fruit if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winter-garden of evergreens
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a winter garden planted with trees that do not cast leaves so the garden remains cheerful in bleak seasons (November, January).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ivy-covered walls and specimens like laurel, hornbeam, and holly; red berries and persistent foliage give a sense of vernal delight amid winter desolation and provide a retreat for birds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress as a social signal and tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that clothing makes people agreeable objects, distinguishes ranks, and influences reception in company; it can raise the timid and temporarily command attention for the unworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress contributes to social duty and respect; it is often better to dress above one's fortune than below it to gain advantage in society; clothes can conceal imperfections and display beauties, affecting conversation and social success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion repository / archival regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a public repository of past fashions with objects displayed in boxes and maintained by a keeper knowledgeable in clothes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposes: furnish models for concealing defects or enhancing beauties; keep money in the kingdom by reducing foreign travel for dress; provide a reference for scholars to clear obscure passages about costume; reduce railing at youth by showing historical precedents. Practicalities: arrange the building with sex-separated apartments, labeled boxes, and a competent keeper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice-seeking is often performative
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that many who ask advice (particularly about marriage) do so to share pleasing secrets or to display the situation, not to follow counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: giving frank advice risks personal danger or social penalty (example of Philander); recipients often have already made up their minds (a woman rarely asks advice before buying wedding clothes). Counselors should recognize the performative aspect of such inquiries.
